questions.q: What is the relationship between the permutation count P(n,k) and the combination count C(n,k)?
options: C(n,k) = P(n,k) / k!, because each unordered selection corresponds to k! different orderings
There is no general relationship between them
questions.explain: Since each unordered selection of k items can be arranged in k! different orders, dividing the ordered count P(n,k) = n!/(n-k)! by k! removes those orderings and gives the unordered count C(n,k) = n!/(k!(n-k)!).

questions.q: Why does the birthday problem reach a greater than 50% chance of a shared birthday with only 23 people, far fewer than the roughly 183 (half of 365) that naive intuition might suggest?
options: Because birthdays are not actually uniformly distributed across the year
Because the comparison is across all C(23,2)=253 pairs of people, not 23 individual dates against 365, so the number of chances for a match grows much faster than n
Because leap years make shared birthdays twice as likely
The 50% figure is incorrect; it actually requires about 183 people
questions.explain: The relevant count is the number of pairs of people, which grows quadratically with n (253 pairs for n=23), so the chance of at least one matching pair crosses 50% at a much smaller n than naive per-person intuition suggests.

questions.q: In 5-card poker, why is a full house (three of one rank, two of another) rarer than a flush (5 cards of one suit, excluding straight flushes)?
options: A full house isn't actually rarer; the two hands have identical probability

The full house count (13 * C(4,3) * 12 * C(4,2) = 3,744) comes from a tighter double-rank constraint, giving a smaller count than the flush's 4 * C(13,5) - 40 = 5,108, out of the same C(52,5) = 2,598,960 total hands
Flushes are rarer because there are only 4 suits
Full houses are rarer because they require exactly 5 cards while flushes can have fewer
questions.explain: Counting directly gives 3,744 full-house hands versus 5,108 flush hands (excluding straight flushes) out of 2,598,960 total 5-card hands, so a full house (~0.144%) is indeed rarer than a flush (~0.197%), matching standard poker hand rankings.

questions.q: What does the 'stars and bars' formula C(n+k-1, k-1) count?
options: The number of ways to arrange n distinct items in a row
The number of ways to distribute n identical items among k distinct categories (including allowing zero in a category)
The number of prime factorizations of n
The number of ways to choose k items from n without replacement, order mattering
questions.explain: Stars and bars counts non-negative integer solutions to x_1 + x_2 + ... + x_k = n, equivalently the number of ways to split n identical items among k categories, giving C(n+k-1, k-1).

questions.q: How many ways are there to split 10 identical risk-budget units among 4 strategies, with any strategy allowed to receive zero?
questions.explain: Using stars and bars with n=10 and k=4, the count is C(n+k-1, k-1) = C(13,3) = 286.
